summary: Learn R-based tax-benefit modelling, fiscal costing, and household impact analysis. Explore policy scenarios in this practical five-day course.
lede: Fiscal and social policy microsimulation estimates how proposed tax, benefit, or subsidy rules may affect household welfare and public budgets. Government economists, tax and budget analysts, and social-protection teams use it to compare reform scenarios and explain who may gain, who may pay, and the estimated fiscal effects. Training covers preparing and checking household data, building and validating R-based scenarios, and interpreting fiscal costs alongside Gini and poverty measures for policy briefings.
audienceIntro: This course is designed for analysts who assess tax, transfer, subsidy, and social-protection options using household evidence. It suits people who work with policy data and need a practical route from reform assumptions to interpretable fiscal and distributional results. This course is designed for: Government economists estimating household effects of tax and benefit reforms. Tax policy analysts translating proposed rate and threshold changes into model rules. Budget analysts estimating revenue and expenditure effects of policy scenarios. Social-protection policy analysts assessing transfer eligibility and benefit adequacy. Subsidy reform analysts comparing fiscal costs and household incidence. Household survey statisticians preparing weighted microdata for policy analysis. Public finance researchers evaluating distributional impacts of fiscal measures. Development-programme advisers reviewing policy options and model assumptions. Economic modelling specialists validating tax-benefit scenario outputs. Policy evaluation leads presenting household impact evidence to senior officials.
prerequisites: Prior experience working with policy, economic, budget, or household data is recommended. You should have basic statistics and data-handling skills, plus working familiarity with R; coding in R is required for the practical scenario exercises. Bring a laptop with R installed. Access to suitable, anonymized household data is useful but not assumed; exercises focus on an illustrative dataset assembled for practice.
